meta.note: Every fact carries a source URL; missing items are listed in gaps as 'not found'. Work in progress.

news_diet.stat: U.S. adults who get news from social media at least sometimes (often+sometimes)
news_diet.value: 53% (21% often, 32% sometimes); 2020: 53% (23% often, 30% sometimes); 2024: 54% (25% often)
news_diet.source: Pew Research Center, Social Media and News Fact Sheet (pub. Sept 25, 2025; ATP survey Aug 18-24, 2025, n=5,153)

news_diet.stat: U.S. adults who regularly get news on Facebook (trend)
news_diet.source: Pew Research Center, 2025 news fact sheets topline (field Aug 18-24, 2025; 2020 wave Aug 31-Sep 7, 2020)

news_diet.stat: U.S. adults who regularly get news on YouTube (trend)
news_diet.source: Pew Research Center, 2025 news fact sheets topline

news_diet.stat: U.S. adults who regularly get news on Instagram (trend)
news_diet.source: Pew Research Center, 2025 news fact sheets topline

news_diet.stat: U.S. adults who regularly get news on TikTok (trend)
news_diet.value: 20% in 2025; 17% 2024; 14% 2023; 10% 2022; 6% 2021; 3% 2020. Under-30s: 43% (2025) vs 9% (2020). 55% of adult TikTok users regularly get news there (22% in 2020). Democrats/leaners 23% vs Republicans/leaners 17%.
news_diet.source: Pew Research Center topline + short read '1 in 5 Americans now regularly get news on TikTok' (Sept 25, 2025) + '8 facts about Americans and TikTok' (Mar 2, 2026)

news_diet.stat: U.S. adults who regularly get news on X (formerly Twitter) (trend)
news_diet.source: Pew Research Center, 2025 news fact sheets topline; Social Media and News Fact Sheet

news_diet.stat: U.S. adults who regularly get news on other platforms
news_diet.value: Reddit 9% (6% in 2020); Nextdoor 6%; WhatsApp 5%; Threads 3%; Rumble 2%; Truth Social 2%; Bluesky 2%. 55% of Truth Social users regularly get news there.
news_diet.source: Pew Research Center, Social Media and News Fact Sheet (Sept 25, 2025)

news_diet.stat: U.S. adults who get news from podcasts often or sometimes (trend)
news_diet.source: Pew Research Center, Podcasts and News Fact Sheet (pub. Sept 25, 2025; survey Aug 18-24, 2025)

news_diet.stat: U.S. adults who regularly get news from news influencers on social media
news_diet.value: 21% overall; 37% of adults 18-29. Of influencers studied, 27% explicitly right-leaning vs 21% left-leaning; 34% also podcast. (Latest Pew estimate found; a Nov 4, 2025 News Influencers Fact Sheet exists but was not retrieved.)
news_diet.source: Pew Research Center, 'America's News Influencers' (pub. Nov 18, 2024; survey Jul 15-Aug 4, 2024, n=10,658)

news_diet.stat: How often U.S. adults get news from each source ('often'), 2020 vs 2025
news_diet.value: TV 40% -> 32%; news websites/apps 34% -> 27%; social media 23% -> 21%; search engines 23% -> 19%; podcasts 6% -> 10%; AI chatbots (first asked 2025) 2%
news_diet.source: Pew Research Center, 2025 news fact sheets topline

news_diet.stat: U.S. adults who get news from AI chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini)
news_diet.value: 9% at least sometimes (2% often, 7% sometimes), 16% rarely, 75% never
news_diet.source: Pew Research Center, 2025 news fact sheets topline (field Aug 18-24, 2025)

news_diet.stat: U.S. adults who use AI chatbots at all / for getting news
news_diet.value: 49% ever use AI chatbots (33% in 2024, not strictly comparable); 24% daily; 42% use them to search for information; 13% use them to get news
news_diet.source: Pew Research Center, 'Americans and AI 2026' (pub. June 17, 2026; field Feb 17-23, 2026, n=5,119)

news_diet.stat: Voters using AI chatbots for election news/voting information
news_diet.value: About 1 in 5 voters consult AI chatbots for election news and voting; Democrats and Republicans at similar rates (AAPC Foundation survey, September 2026; exact n and dates not reported in article)
news_diet.source: NPR (Maham Javaid), 'People are asking ChatGPT to help them decide how to vote in the midterms', Oct 5, 2026 (via WUNC)

news_diet.stat: Voters who have ever used AI for political information or voting decisions
news_diet.value: 9% of voters; 59% of those users trust its outputs (Rainey Center survey, May 2026; n not reported in article)
news_diet.source: Katie Harbath, Anchor Change, May 28, 2026

news_diet.stat: Reuters Institute DNR 2025 (U.S.): weekly news access by source
news_diet.value: Social media/video networks 54% (first time ahead of TV), TV 50%, news websites/apps 48%; weekly news podcast listening 15% (highest of 48 markets)
news_diet.source: Nieman Lab summary of Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2025 (June 16, 2025)

news_diet.stat: Reuters Institute DNR 2026 (global, 48 markets, ~100k respondents): AI chatbots and creators
news_diet.value: Weekly use of AI chatbots for news 10% (7% in 2025); 1% say AI is main news source; 17% of 18-24s weekly; 27% get some news from news-focused creators/influencers; overall trust in news 37% (lowest since 2015); trust in news from AI chatbots 20%. U.S.-specific 2026 figures: not found (Reuters Institute site not retrievable).
news_diet.source: NewscastStudio summary of Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2026 (report pub. June 16, 2026; article June 18, 2026)

news_diet.stat: Gallup: trust in mass media (great deal/fair amount) - latest
news_diet.value: 33% (Sept 1-17, 2026), up from record-low 28% in 2025; 31% 2024; 40% 2020. 2026 by party: Republicans 22% (8% in 2025), independents 31%, Democrats 50% (51% in 2025). 'None at all' 33% (2026).
news_diet.source: Gallup, 'Trust in News Media Edges Slightly Higher' (pub. Sept 29, 2026; phone, n=1,000, +/-4)

news_diet.stat: Gallup: trust in mass media 2025 (prior record low)
news_diet.value: 28% great deal/fair amount (Sept 2-16, 2025); Republicans 8%, independents 27%, Democrats 51%; 'none at all' 34%
news_diet.source: Gallup, 'Trust in Media at New Low of 28% in U.S.' (pub. Oct 2, 2025)

news_diet.stat: Reuters Institute DNR 2026 (U.S.): trust in news
news_diet.value: 25% of Americans say they trust most news most of the time (down 5 points from 2025); 15% among right-leaning Americans; audience trust in CBS News and Fox News each fell 10 points year-on-year, CNN 6 points. Fieldwork late Jan/early Feb 2026 (~2,000 per market; 97,520 adults in 48 markets).
news_diet.source: Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2026 (published June 16, 2026) - PDF copy hosted by frittord.no; corroborated by Election Law Blog excerpt (June 16, 2026)

news_diet.stat: Reuters Institute DNR 2026 (U.S.): AI chatbots and creators
news_diet.value: U.S. reported no increase in AI-chatbot use for news vs 2025 (global weekly use rose 7%->10%); U.S. named among countries with high reliance on news creators (no U.S. percentage given); share of U.S. respondents paying for online news fell 4 points (possibly sampling error).
news_diet.source: Nieman Lab (June 15, 2026); Election Law Blog excerpt of DNR 2026 (June 16, 2026)

ai_events.actor: President Donald Trump (Truth Social)
ai_events.event: Posted AI-generated deepfake video showing Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer making fabricated profane remarks and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries in a sombrero and mustache, on the eve of / during the federal government shutdown; followed by similar meme images.
ai_events.response: Jeffries called it 'disgusting'/bigoted; Sen. Padilla called it 'a racist AI video'; Schumer reposted a 2011 Trump clip captioned 'No AI necessary.' White House spokeswoman defended it as a 'perfect meme'; VP Vance said 'I think it's funny.' No platform moderation reported.

ai_events.actor: California Gov. Gavin Newsom's press office (@GovPressOffice on X)
ai_events.event: Posted AI-generated deepfake video of VP JD Vance hosting a fake show 'A History of Couches', mocking Vance; framed as a reply to Trump's AI videos. Newsom's office has repeatedly used AI satire against Trump (Reuters calls him the most notable Democratic user of AI video).
ai_events.response: No Vance response reported; whether an AI label was attached not reported.

ai_events.actor: National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC)
ai_events.event: Released 30-second ad on X and YouTube with an AI-generated Chuck Schumer repeating 'Every day gets better for us' (a written quote from an Oct 9 Punchbowl News article, never said on camera).
ai_events.response: Small 'AI GENERATED' watermark; YouTube applied 'Altered or synthetic content' label. NRSC said the words were Schumer's own and Republicans should adapt to AI. UC Berkeley's Hany Farid said it 'crosses a line'; some conservative reporters criticized it as a 'slippery slope.'
ai_events.source: NPR (Shannon Bond, Jude Joffe-Block), Oct 17, 2025 (via WYSO)

ai_events.actor: President Donald Trump (Truth Social)
ai_events.event: Posted a seemingly AI-generated video of himself in a crown flying a 'KING TRUMP' jet and dumping a brown substance on 'No Kings' protesters; White House account shared image of Trump/Vance in crowns and Jeffries/Schumer in sombreros.
ai_events.response: Protest organizers (Indivisible, MoveOn) criticized; White House did not immediately comment.

ai_events.actor: Andrew Cuomo campaign (independent NYC mayoral candidate; former Democratic governor)
ai_events.event: Released then deleted a two-minute AI-generated ad 'Criminals for Zohran Mamdani' during the Oct 22 mayoral debate.
ai_events.response: Widely condemned as racist/Islamophobic (incl. CAIR Action); campaign said it was 'inadvertently launched' and deleted it.

ai_events.date: 2025-11 (per Wikipedia summary citing Access WDUN Nov 12, 2025; Reuters gives no date)
ai_events.actor: Rep. Mike Collins campaign (R, Georgia Senate candidate)
ai_events.event: Released deepfake video of Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) appearing to say he voted to keep the government shut down and mocking farm knowledge.
ai_events.response: Collins spokesperson said campaign would embrace new tactics; Ossoff campaign later told the AJC it would commit to not using deepfakes that misattribute words to opponents.
ai_events.source: Reuters (Joseph Ax, Helen Coster), Mar 28, 2026 (via BreakingNews.ie)

ai_events.actor: Gov. Gavin Newsom (X)
ai_events.event: Posted AI-generated video showing Trump, Defense Secretary Hegseth and deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller in handcuffs ('It's cuffing season'), replying to a White House ICE-arrest video.
ai_events.response: No White House/Republican response reported in article; labeling not reported.

ai_events.actor: Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D, Texas Senate candidate) (Facebook)
ai_events.event: Posted AI video (made by parody channel 'Diaper Diplomacy') depicting herself as a baby accusing 'Baby Trump' of rigging Texas elections; a Feb 8, 2026 ad's crowd image was flagged by detection tools as likely AI-generated (campaign did not say).
ai_events.response: YouTube labeled the video 'Altered or synthetic content.'

ai_events.actor: Ken Paxton and John Cornyn campaigns (R, Texas Senate primary)
ai_events.event: Paxton campaign shared AI video of Cornyn dancing with Rep. Jasmine Crockett (end disclaimer: satire); Cornyn posted undisclosed AI video of Rep. Wesley Hunt as a 'show dog' and AI caricatures of Democrats (Talarico as 'Taxula', 'Franken-Beto'); Cornyn later ran AI ad of Paxton with 'Mistress #1/#2'.
ai_events.response: Texas had no AI-disclosure law (2025 bill stalled in Senate); campaigns declined comment.

ai_events.actor: President Donald Trump (Truth Social)
ai_events.event: Reposted a video segment asserting 2020 election fraud (claims Al Jazeera described as baseless) that ended with an image of Barack and Michelle Obama depicted as apes (source did not confirm AI generation).
ai_events.response: Condemned by Republicans (Sen. Tim Scott, Sen. Ricketts, Rep. Lawler) and Democrats; White House first called it a meme, then said a staffer posted it 'erroneously'; deleted by midday Feb 6; Trump declined to apologize.

ai_events.actor: Republican Committee for Loudoun County, Virginia
ai_events.event: Ran three AI ads targeting Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D), one splicing real State of the Union-response footage with AI video of her voicing positions she did not state.
ai_events.response: Spanberger spokesperson declined comment; committee did not reply.

ai_events.actor: National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC)
ai_events.event: 85-second ad with AI-generated James Talarico (D, Texas Senate nominee) reading his old tweets plus invented commentary he never made; small faint 'AI GENERATED' label.
ai_events.response: Talarico campaign: 'deepfake AI videos to mislead Texans'; Sen. Andy Kim (D-NJ) called for national protections; Hany Farid said disclosure inadequate. NRSC: 'These are Talarico's real words.'

ai_events.actor: Reuters review of 2026 public ads
ai_events.event: Reuters found Republicans using AI deepfake technology in ads more than Democrats this cycle; national Democratic campaign committees had not matched NRSC use; Trump White House had released 'scores' of AI videos/memes (incl. promoting the Iran war).
ai_events.response: 28 states had laws on AI in political ads (Public Citizen); no federal rule.
ai_events.source: Reuters (Joseph Ax, Helen Coster), Mar 28, 2026 (via Honolulu Star-Advertiser / BreakingNews.ie)

ai_events.actor: North Star Dawn PAC (super PAC; alignment not stated; aired during DFL Senate primary of Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan vs Rep. Angie Craig)
ai_events.event: Attack ad on Peggy Flanagan (D/DFL) with an apparently altered image of her reaching for corporate money; Flanagan called it an AI deepfake. Wesleyan Media Project cites it as a synthetic video aired despite Minnesota's deepfake ban (90-day window).
ai_events.response: PAC called deepfake claims 'baseless'; Flanagan consulted counsel; Craig said she opposes AI in political ads. Minnesota law faces two pending court challenges (incl. one by X).
ai_events.source: KSTP (Tom Hauser), June 4, 2026; Wesleyan Media Project via Salon (Oct 6, 2026)

ai_events.actor: Citizens for Sanity (group tied to Ken Paxton and allies per HuffPost)
ai_events.event: Aired undisclosed AI deepfake of James Talarico singing a parody song about transgender people (secondary-source summary).
ai_events.response: Talarico campaign focused on positive ads.
ai_events.source: Wikipedia 'AI-generated content in American politics' summarizing HuffPost (June 9, 2026) (secondary source; primary not retrieved)

ai_events.actor: Wesleyan Media Project (tally of AI-generated/enhanced political ads)
ai_events.event: At least 164 (later 'almost 170') AI-generated or AI-enhanced political ads with ~$80M spending in 2026 (undercount); Republican candidates/pro-GOP groups sponsored 80% of ads and 83% of spending; pro-Democratic sponsors 11% of ads and 14% of spending; 69% of ads (78% of spending) lacked an AI disclaimer; disclosure rates similar in states with AI-ad laws (29%) and without (32%).
ai_events.response: Researchers flag weak enforcement and inconsistent disclaimers; cited polling: 78% of registered voters favor banning deceptive AI content about candidates.
ai_events.source: Wesleyan Media Project release (Sept 4, 2026); Ridout/Fowler/Franz in The Conversation via Salon (Oct 6, 2026)

ai_events.actor: Rep. Derrick Van Orden (R-WI-03) campaign; challenger Rebecca Cooke (D)
ai_events.event: Van Orden online ads used AI-generated likeness of Cooke in fictional scenes (e.g., fabricated conversation with Joe Biden). Cooke's lawyers (Elias Law Group) sent cease-and-desist citing Wisconsin's deepfake law, noting the law's exemption gap for federal candidates.
ai_events.response: Van Orden replied with another AI video (duck character).

ai_events.actor: Russia-linked 'Operation Overload' / 'Matryoshka' network (attributed by Graphika and other researchers)
ai_events.event: Real celebrity footage overlaid with AI-cloned/altered audio attacking Democrats (#AllDemocratsAreCriminals) with fake CNN/BBC/NYT branding; fake TV reports targeting Democratic Senate candidates (Ossoff, Brown, Cooper, Jackson, Pappas, Peltola, El-Sayed, Talarico, Turek) on X and Bluesky.
ai_events.response: CNN objected to branding misuse; some content removed by X, Bluesky and TikTok; celebrities (e.g., Jeri Ryan) told AFP statements were not theirs; NYT reported classified U.S. assessments that the Kremlin again authorized a digital influence campaign aimed mainly at sowing chaos, with no evidence of targeting voting machinery.
ai_events.source: La Voce di New York (Sept 16, 2026); New York Times (Sept 18, 2026, republished by DNYUZ); MEAWW fact check (Sept 16, 2026)

ai_events.actor: Iran-linked network (disrupted by Meta, H2 2026 Adversarial Threat Report)
ai_events.event: 4 Facebook + 31 Instagram accounts posing as U.S. activists/students in D.C., San Diego and Atlanta; AI used to make some memes; anti-Republican memes plus Israel-Palestine and immigration messaging; ~79,400 accounts followed the meme accounts; traffic routed via U.S./Canadian proxies.
ai_events.response: Meta removed the network and shared information with U.S. law enforcement; Meta says it finds generative AI in 'virtually every' influence network it disrupts.

ai_events.actor: State-backed Chinese and Iranian operators; two Israel-based private firms (incl. IntelEye)
ai_events.event: Per NYT reporting, campaigns used freely available Chinese AI models to build autonomous AI agents that created and ran fake-account networks on Instagram, Facebook, X and TikTok; the Iranian accounts posed as ordinary Americans and promoted views critical of the Republican Party (~80,000 followers, active in H1 2026).
ai_events.response: U.S. officials and researchers described them as relatively crude but among the first known end-to-end AI-agent influence operations; IntelEye called its activity a defensive research experiment.
ai_events.source: Anadolu Agency summarizing The New York Times (Sept 19, 2026)

ai_events.actor: Anthropic threat intelligence report (Dec 2025-Aug 2026)
ai_events.event: Examined nine influence operations (Russia, Iran, Turkey, Gulf, South Asia, Africa, Europe); incl. a French 'influence-as-a-service' firm (LKM) running 70 fake news sites, 70 X accounts and 250+ comment accounts publishing 8,913 articles in 20 languages targeting the U.S., Brazil, France and DR Congo, with client-driven political direction.
ai_events.response: Accounts banned by Anthropic (per report framing); no U.S.-midterm-specific targeting detailed in summary.

ai_events.actor: Unknown creators (later linked to Russia-linked Operation Overload per NYT/Graphika)
ai_events.event: Viral fake celebrity videos (Alyson Hannigan, Emma Caulfield, Eric Roberts, Jeri Ryan, Sarah Jessica Parker, Julia Roberts) with CNN logo criticizing Democrats spread on X and Instagram; built from repurposed Cameo/ad footage with fake audio.
ai_events.response: AFP and MEAWW fact checks rated them false; celebrities denied the statements.

ai_events.actor: States United Democracy Center study of ChatGPT and Google AI election answers (6 swing states, ~1,000 responses, 2025 and 2026 rounds)
ai_events.event: 2025 round: 6.9% of Google AI and 8.2% of ChatGPT responses had verifiable factual errors; 2026 follow-ups in AZ, PA, MI: zero factual errors; but ChatGPT gave incomplete lists of gubernatorial primary candidates 88.9% of the time and responses linked to official state election sites <40% of the time.
ai_events.response: Google began showing only links (no AI summaries) for election queries in Incognito mode in Feb 2026.

ai_events.actor: U.S. federal government (DOJ/FBI, State Dept, ODNI, CISA)
ai_events.event: Capacity to track foreign influence reduced: AG Pam Bondi disbanded the FBI Foreign Influence Task Force (Feb 2025); State Dept closed its counter-disinformation office (Apr 2025); DNI Gabbard announced the ODNI Foreign Malign Influence Center would be folded into other functions and sunset by end of 2028 (Aug 20, 2025); 'sweeping cuts' at CISA.
ai_events.response: Officials called FMIC 'redundant'; Atlantic Council DFRLab's Emerson Brooking said it is being ended 'in all but name.'

ai_events.actor: Rep. Josh Gottheimer (D, New Jersey governor primary)
ai_events.event: TV ad depicted Gottheimer as a shirtless boxer sparring with Trump (AI-generated imagery per secondary summary).
ai_events.response: Drew attention and criticism.
ai_events.source: Wikipedia 'AI-generated content in American politics' summarizing NBC News and New Jersey Globe (Apr 28, 2025) (secondary source; primary not retrieved)

ai_events.actor: Spencer Pratt (Los Angeles mayoral candidate; described by NPR as Republican-aligned)
ai_events.event: Reposted an AI video portraying himself as Batman and Mayor Karen Bass, Gov. Newsom and Kamala Harris as unruly aristocrats.
ai_events.response: Bass spokesperson said Pratt was 'doing his best Trump impression'; Bass said such AI ads are 'taking on a violent trend'.
ai_events.source: Wikipedia summary citing Newsweek (May 1, 2026), Hollywood Reporter (May 6, 2026), The Hill (May 13, 2026) (secondary source; primary not retrieved); NPR (June 7, 2026) for Pratt's alignment

rules.item: FEC: AI in campaign ads - declined rulemaking on Public Citizen petition; adopted interpretive rule that the fraudulent-misrepresentation ban (52 U.S.C. 30124; 11 CFR 110.16) is technology-neutral and applies to AI-assisted media case by case
rules.status: In effect; no AI-specific FEC rule. No 2025-2026 FEC AI action found.

rules.item: FEC quorum: Commission has lacked a four-member quorum since April 30, 2025 (only Democrats Shana Broussard and Dara Lindenbaum remain after Trey Trainor left Oct 3, 2025); Trump nominated Republicans Ashley Stow and Andrew Woodson on Feb 11, 2026
rules.status: No Senate confirmation found. FEC filed a notice of lack of quorum in Seegers v. FEC on Apr 24, 2026 (https://www.fec.gov/documents/6164/seegers-v-fec-fec-notice-lack-quorum_04-24-26.pdf); Boston Globe (June 13, 2026) reported the FEC had two acting commissioners of six seats; FEC commissioners page (accessed Oct 11, 2026) lists only Broussard and Lindenbaum without end dates - i.e., no quorum apparent. Without a quorum the FEC cannot open enforcement matters, issue advisory opinions or make rules.
rules.source: LobbyComply/State & Federal Communications (Feb 12, 2026); Perkins Coie update; FEC commissioners page; FEC court filing (Apr 24, 2026); Boston Globe (June 13, 2026); FEC commissioners page https://www.fec.gov/about/leadership-and-structure/commissioners/

rules.item: FCC: proposed rule (MB Docket 24-211) requiring on-air and political-file disclosure of AI-generated content in broadcast political ads (no ban)
rules.status: Proposed July 25, 2024 on party-line vote; then-Commissioner (now Chairman) Brendan Carr dissented calling it 'a recipe for chaos'. No final rule adopted; no 2025-2026 adoption found (formal withdrawal status: not found).

rules.item: FCC/TCPA enforcement on AI-voice robocalls: $6M FCC fine on consultant Steve Kramer for the Jan 2024 AI Biden-voice New Hampshire robocalls; Lingo Telecom $1M settlement. Kramer acquitted by NH jury of 11 felony voter-suppression and 11 impersonation charges (June 13, 2025) and said he would not pay the FCC fine.
rules.status: Criminal case ended in acquittal; FCC fine collection status not found.

rules.item: No federal statute or regulation specifically governs AI in political messaging (as of March 2026); bipartisan bills face First Amendment objections
rules.status: No federal AI political ad law

rules.item: States with enacted laws on deepfakes/AI in election communications
rules.status: 33 states have at least one enacted law per Public Citizen tracker (last updated Oct 5, 2026): AL, AZ, CA, CO, DE, FL, HI, ID, IN, KY, LA, ME, MD, MA, MI, MN, MS, MT, NV, NH, NM, NY, ND, OR, PA, RI, SD, TN, TX, UT, VT, WA, WI. Caveats: Hawaii SB 2687 marked 'struck down'; Massachusetts law sunset Feb 2025; California AB 2839/AB 2655 struck down in federal court (Aug 2025); Virginia bills vetoed; Illinois provision integrated into omnibus May 2026. Most laws require disclosure rather than ban. Other counts: 28 states (Public Citizen via Reuters, Mar 2026); 'roughly half' (NCSL via CNN, Mar 2026).
rules.source: Public Citizen, Tracker: State Legislation on Deepfakes in Elections

rules.item: Wisconsin deepfake law's federal-candidate gap: Rebecca Cooke (D, WI-03) cease-and-desist to Rep. Derrick Van Orden argued his online AI ads exploit a loophole not applying to federal candidates
rules.status: Letter sent ~Sept 30, 2026; no legal action reported

rules.item: Kohls v. Bonta (E.D. Cal., Senior Judge John Mendez): California AB 2655 (platform takedown duties) held preempted by Section 230; AB 2839 (election deepfake restrictions) held to fail strict scrutiny under the First Amendment. Plaintiffs incl. parody creator Christopher Kohls ('Mr Reagan'), X Corp., The Babylon Bee.

Kohls v. Ellison (8th Cir.): affirmed denial of preliminary injunction against Minnesota's election deepfake law (Minn. Stat. 609.771); Kohls lacked standing (his videos labeled parody), Rep. Mary Franson had standing but 16-month delay weighed against relief
rules.status: Law remains in force; rehearing en banc denied; case back in district court and held for coordination with X Corp.'s 2025 challenge (pending)
rules.source: Volokh Conspiracy/Reason (Feb 9, 2026); Hamilton Lincoln Law Institute case page

rules.item: Meta: end of U.S. third-party fact-checking, replaced with crowdsourced Community Notes (modeled on X); loosened rules on topics like immigration and gender; warning overlays replaced with labels
rules.status: Announced Jan 7, 2025; Community Notes testing began March 2025; fact-checkers stopped rating new U.S. content April 7, 2025 (Facebook, Instagram, Threads); notes do not reduce distribution
rules.source: AP via PBS NewsHour (Jan 7, 2025); FOX TV Digital (Apr 4, 2025)

rules.item: Meta 2026 midterm policies: 'AI info' labels using C2PA/industry signals and self-disclosure; mandatory disclosure of photorealistic AI video/realistic audio in organic posts; advertisers must disclose AI-created/altered political & social-issue ads; from June 1, 2026 'About this ad' shows when Meta detects third-party AI tools; no new political/issue ads in final week before Election Day; Community Notes; voter-interference removals; Ad Library (7-year retention)
rules.source: Meta newsroom, 'Meta prepares for 2026 US midterms'

rules.item: Google/YouTube 2026 midterm policies: election advertisers must be verified and disclose synthetic or digitally altered content; YouTube creators must disclose AI content (labeled) and YouTube added automatic AI labels; SynthID watermarking and C2PA; election tools in Search/AI Mode/Gemini linking to official info; privacy tool to remove AI imagery of candidates/journalists
rules.status: In effect (announced Sept 9, 2026); no final-week ad restriction mentioned
rules.source: Google blog (Laurie Richardson), 'How we're supporting the 2026 U.S. midterm elections'

rules.item: YouTube: offered reinstatement path for creators banned under retired COVID-19 and election-integrity misinformation policies (Alphabet letter to House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan)
Google AI: began showing only links (no AI-written summaries) for election queries in Incognito mode

X: political ads allowed in the U.S. since reversal of Twitter's 2019 ban (X pledged screening of eligible advertisers and to expand safety/election teams); relies on Community Notes rather than professional fact-checking; labels some AI content
rules.status: Political ads allowed since Aug 29, 2023; 2026-specific X election policy page not retrievable (help.x.com blocked) - details not found

rules.item: TikTok U.S. ownership change: TikTok USDS Joint Venture LLC (Oracle, Silver Lake, MGX 15% each; affiliates of existing ByteDance investors ~30.1%; ByteDance 19.9%; 7-member majority-American board); recommendation algorithm licensed from ByteDance and to be retrained on U.S. data; ByteDance keeps TikTok Shop/advertising operations
rules.status: Deal finalized ~Jan 22, 2026 (reported complete Jan 23, 2026). Days later (Jan 25-26) users alleged suppression of posts on an ICE shooting in Minneapolis; TikTok blamed a data-center power outage; White House said it was not involved in moderation; On Jan 26, 2026 Gov. Newsom asked the California DOJ to investigate whether TikTok suppressed Trump-critical content (Straight Arrow News, Jan 27, 2026: https://san.com/cc/newsom-launches-tiktok-censorship-probe-after-trump-ice-post-complaints/).
rules.source: Gray DC via WKYT (Jan 23, 2026); GuruFocus via Yahoo Finance (Dec 19, 2025); AP via Anchorage Daily News (~Jan 26, 2026); Straight Arrow News (Jan 27, 2026)

rules.item: Paid-influencer disclosure rules: California FPPC regulation (2024) requires paid creators' content to state that the committee paid them; Texas Ethics Commission voted 7-0 in 2024 to require disclosure of paid influencer content; Massachusetts requires disclaimers for social-media marketing >$250 but no influencer-specific rule. Federal: no FEC requirement (2023 internet rule exempted influencer posts on own accounts); Rep. Mark Takano introduced the Promoting Authenticity with Influencer Disclaimers Act on June 2, 2026.
rules.status: State rules in effect in CA/TX; federal bill pending; CLC petition (Oct 2025) to FEC unanswered

rules.item: CFTC proposed rule (Regulation 40.11) defining 'gaming' to exclude elections, awards and other contests, with contract-by-contract public-interest review weighing manipulation and insider-misuse risks (relevant to election prediction markets)
rules.status: Proposed June 10, 2026; comments closed July 27, 2026; final rule not found

rules.item: Prediction-market affiliate rules: after the June 2026 Los Angeles primary, Kalshi barred affiliate creators from questioning election integrity or undermining official election determinations; Polymarket removed some 'paid partnership' tags and says its guidelines bar false or misleading information (no election-specific ban). Kalshi says it bars political staff from betting on their own races.
rules.source: NPR (June 7, 2026, via Texas Public Radio); NPR (Aug 28, 2026, via KUNC)

persuasion.study: Lin et al., 'Persuading voters using human-artificial intelligence dialogues' (with Rand and co-authors; pre-registered experiments around 2024 U.S. presidential, 2025 Canadian federal and 2025 Polish presidential elections, plus a Massachusetts ballot measure)
persuasion.finding: Short multi-turn conversations with an LLM advocating for a candidate shifted preferences; persuasion stronger on out-partisans than mobilizing supporters; effects fell sharply when bots were barred from using facts/evidence; most claims accurate, but bots advocating right-leaning candidates made more inaccurate claims in all three countries. n = 2,300+ (US) + 1,530 (Canada) + 2,118 (Poland) = ~5,948 (US figure approximate).
persuasion.effect_pp: US: ~2-3 points on a 0-100 candidate preference scale on average; pro-Harris bot moved likely Trump voters 3.9 points, pro-Trump bot moved likely Harris voters 1.51 points (described as ~4x larger than effects of ads tested in 2016/2020). Canada and Poland: ~10 percentage points among opposition voters. Massachusetts psychedelics ballot measure: double-digit shifts on 0-100 scale.
persuasion.durability: US: roughly one-third of the effect persisted at a one-month follow-up.

persuasion.study: Hackenburg et al., 'The levers of political persuasion with conversational AI' (Oxford Internet Institute / UK AI Security Institute)
persuasion.finding: 19 LLMs, 707 UK political issues, 91,000+ conversations, 466,769 fact-checkable claims. Conversation beat static messages (GPT-4o +41%, GPT-4.5 +52%). Post-training (reward modeling) and 'information-dense' prompting were the biggest levers (+0.30 pts per additional fact-checkable claim); model scale mattered less (~+1.6 pts per 10x compute); personalization added only +0.43 pts. Trade-off: more persuasive configurations were less accurate (overall 81% of claims accurate; max-persuasion configuration 29.7% inaccurate claims vs 16.0% average).
persuasion.effect_pp: Average treatment conditions ~9.4 pts on 0-100 agreement scale; GPT-4o conversation +2.94 pp and GPT-4.5 +3.60 pp over static messages; maximally persuasive configuration estimated 15.9 pts overall and 26.5 pts among initial disagreers (Cornell summary: ~25 pp among opposition).
persuasion.durability: 36% (chat 1) and 42% (chat 2) of the immediate effect remained at one-month follow-up (Study 1).

persuasion.study: Vargiu & Nai, 'AI chatbots can persuade voters' (News & Views commentary on Lin et al. and Hackenburg et al.)
persuasion.finding: Notes chatbot conversation effects are larger than the average effect of political advertising, which typically shifts vote choice by less than one percentage point.
persuasion.effect_pp: Context: ads typically <1 pp on vote choice

persuasion.study: Cornell Chronicle summary of the Dec 2025 Nature and Science papers
persuasion.finding: Summarizes both papers: Nature sample >2,300 Americans, 1,530 Canadians, 2,118 Poles; Science ~77,000 UK participants on 700+ issues; most persuasion-optimized model shifted opposition voters by 25 pp; more persuasive models were less accurate.
persuasion.effect_pp: US pro-Harris 3.9 pts; pro-Trump 1.51 pts; Canada/Poland ~10 pp; UK max 25 pp among opposition

persuasion.study: Salvi, Horta Ribeiro, Gallotti & West, 'On the conversational persuasiveness of GPT-4' (pre-registered online debates on sociopolitical issues)
persuasion.finding: GPT-4 given basic demographic data about its opponent was more persuasive than humans: in 64.4% of non-tied debates the AI did better, ~81% higher odds of shifting opinion vs human-human baseline; without personalization, GPT-4 was not significantly better than humans.

persuasion.study: Costello, Pennycook & Rand, 'Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI'
persuasion.finding: Personalized GPT-4 Turbo dialogues reduced belief in participants' chosen conspiracy theory by ~20% on average.
persuasion.durability: Persisted undiminished for at least 2 months.

persuasion.study: Chen, Kalla, Le, Nakamura-Sakai et al., 'A Framework to Assess the Persuasion Risks Large Language Model Chatbots Pose to Democratic Societies'
persuasion.finding: Two survey experiments plus a real-world simulation: LLMs are about as persuasive as actual campaign ads once voters are exposed; estimated cost per persuaded voter $48-$74 for LLM persuasion vs ~$100 for traditional campaign methods including exposure costs; traditional methods currently easier to scale.
persuasion.durability: Long-run effects assessed; figures not found

persuasion.study: BASELINE: Kalla & Broockman, 'The Minimal Persuasive Effects of Campaign Contact in General Elections: Evidence from 49 Field Experiments'
persuasion.finding: Meta-analysis of 40 field experiments plus 9 new ones: best estimate of the persuasive effect of campaign contact and advertising on general-election candidate choice is zero; exceptions when candidates take unusually unpopular positions and campaigns target persuadables, or contact long before Election Day (which decays).
persuasion.durability: Early persuasion decays before Election Day

persuasion.study: BASELINE: Coppock, Hill & Vavreck, 'The small effects of political advertising are small regardless of context, message, sender, or receiver' (49 ads from 2016 presidential campaign, 59 experiments)
persuasion.finding: Small average effects with little heterogeneity by tone, timing, partisanship or battleground status; favorability +0.049 points on 1-5 scale.

persuasion.study: BASELINE: Gerber, Gimpel, Green & Shaw, 'How Large and Long-lasting Are the Persuasive Effects of Televised Campaign Ads?' (randomized TV/radio ad timing across Texas media markets, Rick Perry 2006)
persuasion.finding: TV ads had sizable short-run effects; radio had no significant effect.
persuasion.effect_pp: ~4.73 pp average during ad weeks; up to ~6 pp at maximum TV volume
persuasion.durability: Effect -0.17 pp the week after ads ended; vanished before the primary

polling.item: Westwood (Dartmouth), 'The potential existential threat of large language models to online survey research'
polling.finding: An autonomous AI 'synthetic respondent' evaded standard quality checks (attention checks, behavioral flags, response-pattern analysis, 'reverse shibboleth' items) 99.8% of the time, mimicking reading times, mouse movement and typos; cost ~5 cents per response vs ~$1.50 for humans. In final-week 2024 national polls, 10-52 synthetic respondents could have flipped which candidate led; 55-97 to move results outside the margin of error. Recommends identity validation, transparency, controlled recruitment (address-based sampling, voter files).
polling.source: PNAS (Nov 2025); 404 Media (Nov 17, 2025); Campaigns & Elections (Max Greenwood, Nov 24, 2025)

polling.item: Pew Research Center: 'Online opt-in polls can produce misleading results, especially for young people and Hispanic adults'
polling.finding: In a Feb 2022 opt-in experiment, 12% of adults under 30 (and 24% of self-identified Hispanic opt-in respondents vs 2% of non-Hispanics) claimed a license to operate a nuclear submarine (true share ~0%). A Dec 2023 opt-in poll's finding that 20% of under-30s agree 'The Holocaust is a myth' fell to 3% on Pew's probability-based ATP (Jan 16-21, 2024, n=5,140).

polling.item: Pew Research Center: 'No easy fix for bogus respondents in online opt-in polls'
polling.finding: Single opt-in survey (n=11,114, fielded Nov 14-19, 2024): 18% answered 'yes' to at least one impossible-activity trap question; nearly half failed at least one CloudResearch Sentry prescreen check; only 36% could be matched to the voter file. Removing flagged cases improved quality somewhat but no method fixed bias; voter-file matching slightly increased error. Unscreened sample showed a 48-48 presidential tie (Trump underestimated by ~2); screened versions moved to Harris +3 to +7 (bogus respondents tended to claim voting for the winner). Only ~1% of open-ends flagged as 'probable AI', but Pew cautioned subtler AI likely went undetected. Probability panels generally not affected.

polling.item: Pew Q&A: 'Do AI and bogus respondents threaten polling's future?' (Courtney Kennedy)
polling.finding: AI-faked responses mainly threaten opt-in surveys; hypothetical: five bot accounts taking 200 $1 surveys/day could earn ~$30,000/month vs ~$22/month for an AI respondent on Pew's panel. Opt-in can match probability polls on broad measures (e.g., presidential approval) but errs for young adults and rare behaviors. Pew does not use 'silicon sampling' (AI-simulated respondents).

polling.item: AAPOR 2026 Code of Professional Ethics and Practices (amended by members June 2026)
polling.finding: AI-generated/synthetic responses 'are not research participants' and must be identified as AI-created; terms like 'survey'/'poll' should not describe AI-created data; researchers must disclose AI use in data collection/processing (task performed and human oversight) and state whether samples are probability-based, non-probability (opt-in, volunteer) or AI-generated; non-probability reports must omit precision measures unless supported by a detailed model.
polling.source: AAPOR, 2026 Code of Ethics (final PDF); AAPOR call for comments

polling.item: AAPOR Task Force on 2024 Pre-Election Polling
polling.finding: 611 final-two-week polls: average absolute error on two-party margin 3.3 pts (5.3 in 2020, 5.2 in 2016); polls overstated Democratic margins by 2.7 pts across offices (4.6 in 2020, 3.1 in 2016) - third straight presidential cycle underestimating Republicans; no evidence of herding; no consistent pattern of accuracy by method/mode (IVR lowest error, not significant); opt-in panels and RDD frames underrepresent Republican-leaning populations. Report does not tally polls by mode or discuss bots/AI.

polling.item: Mode tally of public pollsters (latest found; no 2026-specific tally found)
polling.finding: Of 78 national public pollsters in 2022: 32% used live phone (alone or combined; 10% live phone only), 33% used probability-based panels (23 pollsters; ~10% in most of the 2010s), 13% used text messaging (9 pollsters), 39% used multiple methods; online opt-in used by 47 pollsters in 2020 (10 in 2012) and roughly flat by 2022. AAPOR estimated 84% of polls before the 2020 election used online methods (56% in 2016).
polling.source: Pew Research Center, 'How Public Polling Has Changed in the 21st Century' (Kennedy, Popky, Keeter)

polling.finding: Verasight (online panel vendor used by Strength In Numbers) describes safeguards: paid-carrier U.S. mobile verification (no VoIP), voter-file/public-record checks, location/VPN checks, throttling survey frequency, cross-survey quality tracking (vendor claims, not independently verified). Pew emphasizes probability sampling via mail, one account per person, web+phone options. No industry-wide 2026 methodological shift documented in sources found.

polarization.measure: Split-ticket House districts (won by one party's presidential candidate and the other party's House candidate)
polarization.value: 2024: 16 (13 Democrats in Trump-won districts, 3 Republicans in Harris-won districts); 2020: 16 (9 R in Biden districts, 7 D in Trump districts); 2022 (2020 presidential lines): 23 (18 R in Biden seats, 5 D in Trump seats); 2012: 26
polarization.trend: Near post-war lows: ~five dozen or more per cycle in the 2000s; never more than ~three dozen since the 2012 redistricting. 2024 was the first presidential year since 2008 with more Democratic than Republican crossover seats.
polarization.source: Kyle Kondik, Sabato's Crystal Ball (via Rasmussen Reports), Jan 16, 2025; Crystal Ball (2020/2022 figures)

polarization.measure: Senate races won by party different from state's presidential winner
polarization.value: 2024: 4 of 34 (~12%: Democratic wins in Trump-carried AZ, MI, NV, WI); 2016: 0 of 34; 2020-2022 combined: ~2. Since 2012, 91% of Senate contests (222 of 245) went to the party that carried the state in the most recent presidential race.
polarization.trend: Down sharply from the 1980s (mismatch rate 59% in 1986), though 2024 ticked up vs 2016-2022.

polarization.measure: District-level correlation between presidential and House vote
polarization.value: 0.987 in 2020 (Gary Jacobson, cited by Crystal Ball). 2024 coefficient: not found.
polarization.trend: Near one-to-one correspondence between House and presidential margins since the 1990s and especially since 2010 (Abramowitz).
polarization.source: Sabato's Crystal Ball (centerforpolitics.org, early 2024, undated in retrieved text); Alan Abramowitz, Crystal Ball via Rasmussen Reports (Feb 12, 2026)

polarization.measure: Share of House districts / states that are presidential swing seats
polarization.value: Highly competitive at presidential level: ~7% of House districts this decade (about one-third in the 1970s); 16% of states (40%+ in the 1970s). Districts deviating 10+ pts from national margin: 80%+ this decade (under one-third in 1970s). Generic-ballot correlation with national House vote .89; Senate .75.
polarization.source: Alan I. Abramowitz, 'It Don't Mean a Thing if it Ain't Got That Swing' (Crystal Ball, via Rasmussen Reports, Feb 12, 2026)

polarization.measure: Voter switching between presidential elections (validated voters)
polarization.value: 2020->2024: 85% of Trump 2020 voters backed him again (11% didn't vote, 4% voted Harris/other); 79% of Biden 2020 voters backed Harris (15% didn't vote, 6% Trump/other); ~3/4 of eligible adults did the same thing in 2024 as 2020; a 'relatively small share' switched parties - turnout differences mattered more.
polarization.trend: Small persuadable/switching share; composition and turnout drive change
polarization.source: Pew Research Center, 'Behind Trump's 2024 Victory' (validated voters, June 26, 2025)

polarization.measure: ANES affective polarization (feeling thermometer toward parties, 0-100)
polarization.trend: Out-party warmth roughly halved since 1978 while in-party warmth is flat - rising affective polarization through 2024
polarization.source: University of Arizona Voter Project summary of ANES Time Series (1978-2024)

polarization.measure: Partisan gap in presidential approval (Gallup, last readings before Gallup stopped)
polarization.value: Nov 3-25, 2025: Trump approval 36% overall; Republicans 84% (second-term low), Democrats 3% (~81-pt gap); independents at worst rating of either term. Gallup announced in Feb 2026 it would no longer publish approval of individual political figures after 88 years.
polarization.trend: Very stable, highly polarized approval; prior three months 40-41% overall
polarization.source: FOX TV Digital (Nov 29, 2025); CNN Newsource via WNEM (Feb 13, 2026)

polarization.value: AP-NORC June 11-17, 2026: 37% (unchanged from May; 36% in early Feb before the Iran war). Reuters/Ipsos: 33% (Aug 28-31, 2026, record low of his career) then 35% (mid-Sept 2026); Reuters/Ipsos generic ballot D 44% - R 37%.
polarization.trend: Narrow range in the mid-to-high 30s during 2026

polarization.measure: Party identification: share of Americans identifying as independents (Gallup annual average)
polarization.value: 45% in 2025 (record; prior high 43% in 2014, 2023, 2024); Democrats +8 over Republicans in identification incl. leaners; 56% of Gen Z identify as independent
polarization.trend: Rising nominal independence even as voting behavior remains highly partisan

polarization.measure: Poll error/bias context (relevant to nationalized forecasting)
polarization.value: 2024 final-two-week polls overstated Democratic margins by 2.7 pts on average across offices (4.6 in 2020; 3.1 in 2016); avg absolute error 3.3 pts
polarization.trend: Third straight presidential cycle underestimating Republicans (midterm 2022/2018 not covered here)
polarization.source: AAPOR Task Force on 2024 Pre-Election Polling (Oct 2025)

money.item: AdImpact 2025-26 cycle political ad spending projection (updated)
money.value: $11.6B (up from $10.8B initial Sept 2025 projection); most expensive cycle on record vs $11.2B in 2023-24 and $8.9B in 2021-22. Spend through June 1, 2026: $4.0B (vs $2.7B at same point in 2024 and 2022).

Broadcast TV $5.6B (48%); CTV/OTT $2.7B (23%; exec summary says $2.6B); digital $1.6B (~14%); cable $1.4B (12%); radio $273M (~2%); satellite $88M (~1%). Original Sept 2025 projection: broadcast $5.3B, CTV $2.5B, digital $1.4B, cable $1.1B.

Senate $3.4B; governor $2.4B; House $2.0B (record; 2024 peak $1.7B); downballot $3.0B; state legislature $698M. Top states: California $979M, Michigan $852M, Texas $850M, Ohio $749M, Georgia $700M, North Carolina $510M, Maine $491M, Pennsylvania $381M.

money.item: Most expensive 2026 races by ad spending (AdImpact, as of Sept 22, 2026)
money.value: Ohio Senate ~$197M; Texas Senate ~$140M; Maine Senate ~$110M (NC, GA, MI, IA also expected in top 10)
~$80M on ~164-170 AI-generated/enhanced ads tracked in 2026 (undercount); 83% of that spending pro-Republican, 14% pro-Democratic

money.item: Paid influencer/creator spending in 2026 campaigns (examples, both parties)
money.value: NRCC (R) paid $120,000+ to conservative influencer network Creator Grid in 2025-26 (labeled 'media'); Tom Steyer (D, CA governor primary) hired creator Carlos Eduardo Espina as consultant for $100,000 and reportedly paid TheShadeRoom $25,000 for one post, plus $1,000/month creator listings, without disclosure in original posts (FPPC complaint filed); Democratic Senate campaigns of Seth Moulton (MA), Mallory McMorrow and Haley Stevens (MI) spent 'thousands' with agency Good Influence. Rep. Mark Takano introduced the Promoting Authenticity with Influencer Disclaimers Act (June 2, 2026). Aggregate 2026 influencer spending total: not found.

FEC's 2023 internet disclaimer rule exempted paid influencer posts on creators' own accounts; PACs need not name creators paid through intermediary agencies; Campaign Legal Center and others petitioned FEC in Oct 2025 to close the gap (no action; FEC lacks quorum). Prior-cycle benchmarks: DNC + Harris campaign paid >$4M to one influencer agency in 2024; a Democratic-aligned PAC paid $5,000-$15,000 per post (>=$1M total); Chorus (Democratic-aligned) offered creators $8,000/month with non-disclosure terms (WIRED, 2025); Trump campaign spent $1.8M on influencer marketing in 2020 and in 2024 gave non-cash perks (credentials, access) to pro-Trump creators.

NYT reported campaigns see paid influencer endorsements as cheaper than traditional ads; federal rules don't require disclosure and only a few states do; some creators said campaigns asked them to hide payments (no dollar totals given)
money.source: Political Wire summarizing The New York Times (Aug 29, 2026)

markets_media.item: X named Polymarket its 'official prediction market partner'; planned integrated product combining Polymarket probabilities with X data and real-time Grok annotations of market moves.
Google announced Google Finance would add Polymarket and Kalshi prediction-market probabilities (gradual rollout starting with Google Labs users).

Polymarket became Yahoo Finance's exclusive (sole) prediction-market data partner; a hub pairing Polymarket probabilities on economic, government and market outcomes with Yahoo Finance news was to launch 'in the coming months'.

CNN struck an exclusive prediction-data partnership with Kalshi: real-time API data shown via on-air ticker; chief data analyst Harry Enten to use Kalshi insights on TV and streaming; covers politics, news, culture, weather; CNN does not pay for the data and will not work with other prediction markets. Donald Trump Jr. is an adviser to both Kalshi and Polymarket.
CNBC (Versant) signed a multi-year deal starting in 2026 to use real-time Kalshi data across TV and digital, including a Kalshi ticker in some on-air segments ('Squawk Box', 'Fast Money').

Criticism of CNN-Kalshi deal: FAIR's Jim Naureckas said it could open the door to political manipulation and encourage horse-race coverage; Campaign for Accountability called prediction markets 'just another form of gambling'. CNN did not comment.
Polymarket agreed to supply real-time probability data to Dow Jones outlets (Wall Street Journal, Barron's, MarketWatch, Investor's Business Daily) via digital modules and some print editions.

Los Angeles mayoral primary: paid Kalshi/Polymarket affiliate influencers on X cited shifting betting odds as 'evidence' of fraud during the slow count (markets had favored Spencer Pratt for second place though large likely-voter polls had him third); AP called second place for Nithya Raman June 8. Kalshi told affiliates to delete posts and now bars affiliates from questioning election integrity; Polymarket removed 'paid partnership' tags from some posts. Creators were reportedly paid up to $500/post. LA County registrar said early returns differing from market expectations fed suspicion of ballot processing.
markets_media.source: NPR (Jude Joffe-Block, Bobby Allyn), June 7, 2026 (via Texas Public Radio); AFP via Malay Mail (June 14, 2026); Votebeat (Aug 8, 2026)

markets_media.item: CFTC proposed rule defining 'gaming' under Regulation 40.11 that excludes elections, awards and other contests (i.e., election contracts not treated as prohibited gaming), with contract-by-contract public-interest review considering manipulation and insider-misuse risks; comments due July 27, 2026.

NBC News analysis: nearly $200M traded on midterm outcomes on Kalshi and Polymarket; Wisconsin election officials issued an advisory citing a 19th-century law barring voters from voting in races they bet on (Kalshi called it 'active voter suppression'); Delaware County, PA banned election workers from betting via prediction markets; Pew (June 2026) found most states have some election-betting prohibition.

Anti-Corruption Data Collective analysis of 7,466 congressional markets (data to Aug 10, 2026): $133M wagered on 2026 congressional races (vs $92.4M in entire 2024 cycle), projected up to $1.6B; on Polymarket Global top 1% of wallets = 68% of volume; 10 wallets hold 17% of volume across 426 of 470 seats; 87% of markets thin/low-volume or concentrated; only 39,820 wallets have bet on 2026 congressional races. Warns prices can reflect a few well-funded traders or manipulation.

Fabricated polls from a fake firm ('Median Strategies') on LA mayor, Wisconsin and Nevada races were reported by several outlets as real and promoted by Mayor Karen Bass; creator (Rahil Prakash, per The Guardian) called it a social experiment. Kalshi said markets 'barely reacted' and found no trades by him; cited a study where a $1M+ bet in an LA primary market moved odds for only nine seconds. Better Markets' Amanda Fischer: 'These markets are very easily manipulated.' Insider-trading cases in 2026 cited (e.g., bets tied to the Maduro operation).
